name: Stack from Chill Dog
description: Defending Chill Dog opens the high-leg enclosure before advancing through guard. Forward pressure must not fold the partner onto the neck or wrench the shoulder.
summary: Defending Chill Dog requires a safe base and release of the high-leg enclosure before advancing through the remaining guard.
overview:
The top player faces a bottom guard player using Chill Dog; the head, shoulder or arm may still be enclosed. Forward pressure must not fold the partner onto the neck. The reviewed sources do not establish stacking as a required Chill Dog escape or an automatic Half Guard result.

Keep the free hand available for framing while preventing the isolated elbow from being pulled further away from your torso. The opponent changing the hand around your head signals the move beyond New York, not a turtle escape. Keep a balanced base and early inside frames; tap instead of moving against a completed choke or joint lock.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

Instructional sources: [Brandon McCaghren — Gogoplata from rubber guard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wn39-wrfsbs); [Eddie Bravo — Chill Dog / Invisible Collar clarification](https://www.10thplanetjj.com/forum/threads/17657-Chill-Dog-Invisible-Collar-Question).

defender.name: Stack from Chill Dog Defender
defender.description: Stack from Chill Dog (defender): Keep the opposing hand on the mat and hug the knee before changing the head-side grip. Bring the knee toward the chest through hip movement so the neck-clearing motion does not twist the knee.
defender.overview:
The top player faces a bottom guard player using Chill Dog; the head, shoulder or arm may still be enclosed. Forward pressure must not fold the partner onto the neck. The reviewed sources do not establish stacking as a required Chill Dog escape or an automatic Half Guard result.

Keep the opposing hand on the mat and hug the knee before changing the head-side grip. Bring the knee toward the chest through hip movement so the neck-clearing motion does not twist the knee. Move the controlling arm around the head while keeping the leg and trapped arm connected.

Use the forearm near the shoulder line to manage forward pressure; do not let the frame collapse across your own wrist. Keep the knee hug while choosing further control such as Invisible Collar or an omoplata setup. Return the legs to a comfortable guard if the opponent withdraws the elbow or stacks your upper back.

Move through available space with a stable base. Stop and release any trapped neck, shoulder or knee before changing direction; do not force a roll or stack to preserve the route.

When the high connection must open, use a supported hip escape and a knee returning inside for guard retention. A forearm at the shoulder blocks a crossface and incoming chest pressure while you make that space.
key_principles: Secure New York first: Keep the opposing hand on the mat and hug the knee before changing the head-side grip.
Turn onto the hip: Bring the knee toward the chest through hip movement so the neck-clearing motion does not twist the knee.
Clear the neck: Move the controlling arm around the head while keeping the leg and trapped arm connected.
Place the inside frame: Use the forearm near the shoulder line to manage forward pressure; do not let the frame collapse across your own wrist.
Maintain the arm trap: Keep the knee hug while choosing further control such as Invisible Collar or an omoplata setup.
Recover when control opens: Return the legs to a comfortable guard if the opponent withdraws the elbow or stacks your upper back.
